title: Punctuation Fix-It
subtitle: Tap the correctly-punctuated line. Seven quick dialogue rules.

drills.setup: Maya tells Dev she is heading home. A dialogue tag follows the speech.

options.why: When a tag like “Maya said” follows the speech, use a comma inside the quotes — a period ends the sentence too soon.
The closing punctuation goes INSIDE the quotation marks — this line has none before the tag.

drills.teach: When a dialogue tag follows the speech, the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark and the tag stays lowercase: “…home,” Maya said.

drills.setup: The speech is a question, and a tag follows it.

options.why: A question mark already does the comma’s job — don’t stack “?,” together.
The question mark belongs INSIDE the quotes — the character asked the question, not the narrator.

drills.teach: A question mark (or exclamation point) replaces the comma before a tag, and it lives inside the quotation marks: “Are you sure?” he asked.

drills.setup: The tag comes FIRST, then the speech.

options.why: Put a comma after the tag before the speech opens.
The first word of the spoken line is capitalized — it starts a new sentence of speech.

drills.teach: When the tag leads, put a comma after it, then open quotes and capitalize the first spoken word: She whispered, “Don’t move.”

drills.setup: A tag interrupts one continuous sentence of speech.

options.why: The second half continues the SAME sentence, so “we” stays lowercase.
Periods break it into three sentences — use commas to show one sentence interrupted by the tag.

drills.teach: When a tag splits ONE sentence, wrap it in commas and don’t capitalize the continuation: “I think,” she said, “we should wait.”

drills.setup: An ACTION beat follows the speech — it is a full action, not a speech tag.

options.text: “I’m done.” She pushed back her chair.
“I’m done,” She pushed back her chair.
options.why: “She pushed back her chair” isn’t a speech tag — it’s its own action sentence, so end the speech with a period and capitalize.

options.text: “I’m done,” she pushed back her chair.
options.why: You can’t “push a chair” a line of dialogue — this isn’t a tag like “said”, so it needs a period and a capital.

drills.teach: An action beat is its own sentence, not a tag: end the speech with a period and start the action with a capital — “I’m done.” She pushed back her chair.

drills.setup: An exclamation of speech, with a tag after it.

options.why: Don’t stack “!,” — the exclamation point already ends the spoken part.
The exclamation belongs inside the quotes — Cal shouted it, the narrator didn’t.

drills.teach: Exclamation points work like question marks: inside the quotes, and they replace the comma before the tag — “Watch out!” Cal shouted.

drills.setup: Two characters speak back to back.
drills.prompt: Which is formatted correctly for a two-person exchange?

options.text: “Ready?” Dev asked. / “Almost,” Maya said. (each on a new line)
“Ready?” Dev asked. “Almost,” Maya said. (both on one line)
options.why: Every time the speaker changes, start a NEW paragraph — otherwise the reader loses track of who’s talking.

options.text: “Ready? Almost,” they said. (both voices in one set of quotes)
options.why: Two speakers can’t share one set of quotation marks — split them so each voice is clear.

drills.teach: New speaker, new paragraph. Give each character their own line so the reader always knows who is talking.
